            "prompt": "Study Planner with Free-Slot Finder: Design Doc\nAuthor: Srividya · Status: Draft v0.1 · Date: 22 October 2026\n1. Purpose\nA mobile app where students add tasks with time estimates and set focus goals. The app suggests the best time slot for each task, on a given day or in the week, without causing burnout. Study groups can see common free slots and book them.\nThis is also a learning project. It is built with no AI help, and the app uses no AI. All suggestions come from fixed rules and formulas.\n2. Goals and non-goals\nGoals\n• Work end to end for 10 users.\n• Suggest one slot per task based on schedule, goals, and priority.\n• Enforce burnout limits strictly.\n• Let users edit anything at any time.\n• Teach: Flutter, REST APIs, auth, relational databases, interval algorithms, date and time handling, concurrency, testing, deployment.\nNon-goals (for v1)\n• Any AI or machine learning.\n• Offline mode.\n• Multiple timezones (India only).\n• More than 10 users.\n• Automatic slot suggestions for groups (groups only see free slots and book them).\n3. Decided rules\nRule\nValue\nBlock length\n50 to 60 minutes\nGap after a block\n15 to 25 minutes\nMax blocks per day\n8 (classes and fixed events not counted)\nMax blocks per week\n40\nLimits\nHard, enforced on the backend\nUsers in v1\n10\nConnectivity\nOnline only\nTimezone\nIndia (IST) only\nPriority\nGoal weights and ranking\nRepeating tasks\nUser chooses how often a task repeats\nOverrun\nApp asks the user what to do\nGroups\nShow common free slots, members book\n4. Main user flows\n1. Sign up and log in.\n2. Enter fixed events such as classes.\n3. Set goals and their priority.\n4. Add a task: title, estimate, deadline, linked goal, repeat pattern.\n5. Ask for a suggestion for a day or the week, then accept or change it.\n6. During or after a block, report that a task needs more time.\n7. Join a group, view common free slots, and book one.\n5. v1 features\n• Account and login.\n• Fixed events (one-time and repeating).\n• Goals with weights and ranking.\n• Tasks with estimates, deadlines, and repeat patterns.\n• Slot suggestion for a day or a week.\n• Edit or delete anything, with limits re-checked each time.\n• Overrun handling.\n• Groups: create, join, view common free slots, book.\n• Burnout warnings and rejections with clear reasons.\n6. System overview\nFlutter app, then a REST API (proposed: Go), then a relational database (proposed: PostgreSQL). Both language and database are proposed and need confirming.\nKey principle: the backend is the source of truth. The app only displays and sends requests. Every rule (limits, conflicts, booking) is checked on the backend, because the client cannot be trusted.\nSuggestions are never stored as facts. Only tasks, goals, events, and accepted blocks are stored. Suggestions are recomputed when something changes.\n7. Data model (entities)\nEntity\nPurpose\nKey fields to define\nUser\nAccount\nid, name, login details, day window, settings\nGoal\nFocus area\nowner, name, weight, rank\nTask\nWork to do\nowner, goal, title, estimate, deadline, repeat rule, status\nBlock\nA scheduled work session\ntask, start, end, actual time spent, status\nFixed event\nClass or commitment\nowner, title, start, end, repeat rule\nGroup\nStudy group\nname, members, join method\nGroup booking\nA booked group session\ngroup, start, end, attendees, status\nOpen design points: how to store repeat rules, and whether repeated tasks are stored as one rule or as many rows.\n8. Scheduling: the core problem\nThis section lists the problem. The solution is for me to design and learn.\nInputs: day window, fixed events, existing blocks, tasks with estimates and deadlines, goal weights and ranks, current daily and weekly block counts.\nOutput: one suggested slot for a task, for a day or a week, or a clear reason why none exists.\nConstraints to respect:\n• Blocks are 50 to 60 minutes with a 15 to 25 minute gap.\n• Never overlap fixed events.\n• Never exceed 8 blocks in a day or 40 in a week.\n• Respect the end-of-day cutoff and meal times (to be decided).\n• Tasks longer than a block are split into sessions.\n• Short tasks of the same goal may be batched into one block.\nThings to design:\n• How to compute free time from busy time.\n• How to check that a slot fits a block plus its gap.\n• A scoring formula that combines goal weight, rank, and deadline urgency.\n• How weights and ranks combine into one priority.\n• Tie-breaking rules.\nThe scheduler should be pure logic, separate from the database and the API, so it can be tested alone.\n9. Enforcing hard limits\nEvery action that changes the schedule goes through the same checks: adding a task, editing an estimate, extending an overrun, moving a block, and booking a group slot.\nIf a check fails, the action is rejected with a reason and options: move to another day, shorten the task, or remove another task.\nDecisions needed: when the week starts, and how the day and week are counted in IST.\n10. Overrun flow\n1. User reports that a task needs more time and enters the extra minutes.\n2. The backend checks the daily and weekly limits and the fixed events.\n3. The app shows options: extend the current block, move the rest to the next slot, or postpone.\n4. If the limit would be broken, the extend option is blocked and explained.\n5. If the deadline is at risk, show a warning.\nEach task keeps estimate, time spent, and time remaining. Estimated versus actual time is saved for later use. A per-user average ratio can adjust future estimates (plain arithmetic, no AI).\n11. Group feature\nDecided: the app shows common free slots, and members book one.\nStill to decide:\n• How groups are created and joined (invite code or approval).\n• Whether a user can be in several groups.\n• What members see of each other (only free or busy, or task details). Free or busy only is the safer start.\n• Whether a group session counts toward each member's 8 and 40 block limits.\n• Whether everyone must accept or the first booking wins.\n• Who can cancel or change a booking.\n• How to prevent two people booking the same slot at the same moment (database transactions).\nA slot is only available for a member if booking it would not break that member's limits.\n12. API outline (resources)\nAuth, users, goals, tasks, fixed events, blocks, suggestions, groups, group free slots, group bookings. Each needs: create, read, update, delete where it makes sense, with validation and clear error messages.\n13. Flutter app\nScreens: login, home (day and week view), add or edit task, goals, fixed events, suggestion result, overrun options, groups list, group detail with free slots.\nTo learn and decide: one state management approach, navigation, forms, calling the API, and how to draw a timeline view.\n14. Testing plan\n• Unit tests for the scheduler (most important): empty day, full day, back-to-back events, limit edges, deadlines, ties.\n• Unit tests for limit checks and date handling, including week boundaries.\n• API tests for auth, validation, and rejections.\n• A concurrency test for double booking.\n• Basic widget tests in Flutter.\n• A trial with the 10 real users.\n15. Deployment\nHost the backend and database, set up simple automated tests on each push, build an Android APK for the users, and keep a Git workflow with branches and pull requests.\n16. Learning plan and milestones\n1. Learn interval algorithms and date handling, then build the scheduler as pure logic with tests.\n2. Learn database design and REST, then build the database, auth, and API.\n3. Learn Flutter basics, then build login and the basic screens.\n4. Connect tasks, goals, fixed events, and repeat patterns end to end.\n5. Add suggestions, limit enforcement, and the overrun flow.\n6. Add groups and booking.\n7. Deploy and test with 10 users.\n17. Risks\n• Scheduling rules interacting in unexpected ways. Mitigation: tests first.\n• Repeat patterns growing complex. Mitigation: support only a few patterns in v1.\n• Date and week boundary bugs. Mitigation: one clear rule, tested.\n• Double booking. Mitigation: database transactions.\n• Scope growth. Mitigation: keep to v1 only.\n18. Open questions\n1. Confirm Go and PostgreSQL.\n2. How do weights and ranks combine?\n3. Which repeat patterns are in v1, and how are they stored?\n4. Time rules: smallest time unit, storing UTC and showing IST, when the week starts.\n5. How are classes entered (one-time or weekly)?\n6. Gap rule: 15 minutes by default and 25 after a 60 minute block or the third block in a row (unconfirmed).\n7. Extra burnout rules: meal windows, end-of-day cutoff, rest day.\n8. The exact scoring formula.\n9. All group rules in section 11. check this and lets discuss about this "

          "content": "Reading through the design doc carefully before we discuss.\n\nThe doc is well-structured for a learning project. Let me go through section 11 (group feature) systematically, flagging what's decided, what's genuinely open, and where I'd push back or suggest a direction.\n\n---\n\n## Group Feature Discussion\n\n### What's already solid\n\n- Common free slots are computed, not stored — consistent with the core principle.\n- A slot is only available if booking it won't break a member's limits. Good. This belongs on the backend.\n- Concurrency via database transactions is the right call.\n\n---\n\n### Open questions, one by one\n\n**1. How are groups created and joined?**\n\nInvite code is simpler to implement and teach (generate a random code, store it, validate on join). Approval flows require async state (pending/accepted/rejected) and more API work. For v1 with 10 users who likely know each other, invite code is enough. Keep approval for v2.\n\n**2. Can a user be in several groups?**\n\nPractically yes — students are in multiple study groups. The data model already supports this (Group has members, so it's a many-to-many). There's no scheduling conflict risk since a group booking still checks each member's individual limits. I'd allow multiple groups in v1.\n\n**3. What do members see of each other?**\n\nFree/busy only is the right call for v1. Task details are sensitive (what you're studying, how behind you are). It's also less to build. Start with free/busy and never need to walk it back.\n\n**4. Does a group session count toward each member's 8 and 40 block limits?**\n\nYes, it must. A group session is a real block of focused time. If it doesn't count, users can exceed the burnout limits by packing in group sessions. The backend should treat a group booking exactly like a personal block when checking limits.\n\n**5. Does everyone need to accept, or does first booking win?**\n\nThis is the most architecturally significant question. Two options:\n\n- **First booking wins**: simpler. One member books, it's locked. Others see it as occupied. Risk: someone books a slot others weren't ready for.\n- **All must confirm**: safer socially, but requires a pending state, notifications, and timeout logic. That's a lot of async complexity for v1.\n\nRecommendation: **first booking wins**, but the person who books sees a confirmation screen that says \"this will be booked for the group.\" Keep it simple. Add confirmations in v2 if users ask.\n\n**6. Who can cancel or change a booking?**\n\nTwo reasonable choices: the person who booked it, or any member. \"Any member can cancel\" is more flexible but could cause chaos. \"Only the booker can cancel\" is simpler and more predictable. I'd go with: **only the booker can cancel, any member can propose a change (which the booker then confirms)**. But for v1, simplify further: only the booker can cancel, no change flow — just cancel and rebook.\n\n**7. Double booking prevention**\n\nThe doc already says database transactions. That's correct. The implementation pattern is: wrap the slot availability check and the insert into a single serializable transaction (or use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the relevant rows). This is a good concurrency lesson. Worth calling out explicitly in the learning plan.\n\n---\n\n### Things the doc doesn't address yet that matter\n\n**Who can see the group's free slots?**\nOnly members, presumably. The API needs to enforce this — a non-member calling `GET /groups/{id}/free-slots` should get a 403.\n\n**What is a \"group free slot\" exactly?**\nIt's the intersection of all members' free time, filtered to slots where every member has room under their limits. This is a non-trivial computation: you need to intersect N users' busy intervals. It should follow the same interval logic as the personal scheduler. Worth noting in section 8 that the group free-slot algorithm is a generalisation of the personal one.\n\n**Does a group booking create a Block record for each member?**\nIt should. Otherwise the limit checks won't work — the backend needs a block row per member to count toward their 8/40. The `group_booking` table links them, but individual `block` rows are what the limit checker reads.\n\n**What's the minimum group size?**\nPresumably 2. Worth stating.\n\n**Can a group have a maximum size?**\nNot critical for v1 with 10 users total, but if you have 3 groups of 4 people who all overlap, the intersection might always be empty. Something to mention as a known usability risk, not a blocker.\n\n---\n\n### Suggested decisions for v1\n\n| Question | Recommendation |\n|---|---|\n| Join method | Invite code only |\n| Multiple groups per user | Allowed |\n| Visibility | Free/busy only |\n| Counts toward limits | Yes, always |\n| Booking model | First booking wins |\n| Cancel rights | Booker only; cancel and rebook instead of edit |\n| Concurrency | `SELECT FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction |\n| Block rows | One per member on booking |\n| Min group size | 2 |\n\n---\n\n### One design tension to flag\n\nSection 6 says \"suggestions are never stored as facts.\" Group free slots follow the same rule — they're computed on demand. But a group *booking* is a fact and must be stored. Make sure the data model clearly distinguishes `group_free_slot` (computed, never stored) from `group_booking` (stored, creates block rows). The current entity table has `group_booking` which is right, just make sure there's no temptation to cache the free-slot computation.\n\n---\n\nWhat would you like to dig into further — the concurrency mechanics, the free-slot intersection algorithm, or the booking/block relationship?"

          "tool_uses": [
            {
              "id": "tooluse_0xUN5DiUistS71bL8hT2JS",
              "name": "fs_write",
              "orig_name": "fs_write",
              "args": {
                "command": "create",
                "path": "/home/morampudimahi/Desktop/24wh1a05t5/uid/Planner/decisions.md",
                "file_text": "# Group Feature Decisions\n**Project:** Study Planner with Free-Slot Finder\n**Author:** Srividya\n**Date:** 22 October 2026\n**Status:** Decided — v1\n\n---\n\n## Context\n\nSection 11 of the design doc listed the group feature as partially open. This document records the final decisions for v1, the reasoning behind each, and what is explicitly deferred to v2.\n\n---\n\n## Decisions\n\n### 1. How groups are created and joined\n\n**Decision:** Invite code only.\n\nA group creator generates a short random code. Anyone with the code can join. No approval flow in v1.\n\n**Reasoning:** An approval flow requires async state (pending / accepted / rejected), extra API endpoints, and notification logic. For v1 with 10 known users, an invite code is sufficient. The data cost is one extra field on the Group table.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Approval-based joining, invite expiry, revoke invite.\n\n---\n\n### 2. Can a user be in multiple groups?\n\n**Decision:** Yes, a user can be in any number of groups.\n\n**Reasoning:** The data model already requires a many-to-many join between users and groups. There is no scheduling conflict risk because a group booking is always checked against each member's individual limits before it is confirmed. Restricting this would hurt real use cases with no benefit.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** A per-user group limit if needed.\n\n---\n\n### 3. What do members see of each other?\n\n**Decision:** Free/busy only. No task titles, goal names, or estimates are visible to other members.\n\n**Reasoning:** Task details reveal what a person is studying and how far behind they are. That is sensitive. Free/busy is enough to compute common slots. Starting restrictive is easier to relax later than the reverse.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Optional sharing of task titles within a group, if users ask for it.\n\n---\n\n### 4. Does a group session count toward each member's block limits?\n\n**Decision:** Yes. A group booking counts as one block for every attending member, toward both the 8-block daily limit and the 40-block weekly limit.\n\n**Reasoning:** A group session is real focused time. Excluding it from limits would let users exceed burnout thresholds by filling their schedule with group sessions. The backend's limit checker must see a block row per member; it has no concept of \"group\" vs \"personal.\"\n\n**Implementation note:** When a group booking is confirmed, the backend creates one Block row per attending member. The GroupBooking row links them. Limit checks run before the booking is written.\n\n---\n\n### 5. Booking model — does everyone confirm, or does first booking win?\n\n**Decision:** First booking wins. The first member to book a free slot locks it for the group.\n\n**Reasoning:** A confirmation flow requires a pending state, a notification system, and timeout logic — significant complexity for v1. With 10 known users coordinating casually, first-booking is practical. The booking screen shows a clear confirmation step: \"Book this slot for the group?\" before the request is sent, so it is not accidental.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** All-must-confirm model, booking proposals, notifications.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Who can cancel a booking?\n\n**Decision:** Only the member who made the booking can cancel it. There is no edit flow — cancel and rebook instead.\n\n**Reasoning:** Allowing any member to cancel creates coordination problems (someone cancels without telling others). Only-the-booker is simpler and predictable. An edit flow (change the time) requires re-running availability checks for all members and is equivalent to cancel-and-rebook anyway, so it is not worth building separately in v1.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Any-member cancel with a reason field, booking transfer.\n\n---\n\n### 7. Concurrency — preventing two members booking the same slot simultaneously\n\n**Decision:** Use a database transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the affected rows. The availability check and the insert happen inside a single serializable transaction.\n\n**Reasoning:** Without a lock, two members could both pass the availability check at the same time and both write a booking, resulting in an overbooked slot. `SELECT FOR UPDATE` ensures only one transaction proceeds; the second reads the updated state and fails cleanly with a \"slot no longer available\" error, which the app surfaces to the user.\n\n**Implementation note:** This is a learning objective. The concurrency test in the testing plan (section 14 of the design doc) must cover this case explicitly: simulate two simultaneous booking requests for the same slot and assert that exactly one succeeds.\n\n---\n\n### 8. Block rows on booking\n\n**Decision:** Confirming a group booking creates one Block row per attending member. If group bookings did not produce Block rows, the checker would be blind to them. This is the cleanest way to keep the limit logic simple and uniform — it does not need to know about groups at all.\n\n**Schema implication:**\n\n```\nGroupBooking\n  id\n  group_id\n  start\n  end\n  booked_by (user_id)\n  status\n\nBlock\n  id\n  task_id         -- NULL for a group booking block\n  group_booking_id -- NULL for a personal block; set for group booking blocks\n  user_id\n  start\n  end\n  actual_time_spent\n  status\n```\n\nOne of `task_id` or `group_booking_id` is set; the other is null. The limit checker counts all Block rows for a user regardless of which column is set.\n\n---\n\n### 9. Minimum group size\n\n**Decision:** A group must have at least 2 members before a booking can be made. A group can be created with 1 member (the creator), but the \"view free slots\" and \"book\" actions are disabled until a second member joins.\n\n**Reasoning:** A group session with one person is just a personal block. Group free slots — computation, not storage\n\n**Decision:** Group free slots are always computed on demand and never stored.\n\n**Reasoning:** Consistent with the core principle in section 6 of the design doc: suggestions are never stored as facts. A group free slot is the intersection of all members' free intervals, filtered to times where every member has capacity under their limits. This document records the final decisions for v1, the reasoning behind each, and what is explicitly deferred to v2.\n\n---\n\n## Decisions\n\n### 1. How groups are created and joined\n\n**Decision:** Invite code only.\n\nA group creator generates a short random code. Anyone with the code can join. No approval flow in v1.\n\n**Reasoning:** An approval flow requires async state (pending / accepted / rejected), extra API endpoints, and notification logic. For v1 with 10 known users, an invite code is sufficient. The data cost is one extra field on the Group table.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Approval-based joining, invite expiry, revoke invite.\n\n---\n\n### 2. Can a user be in multiple groups?\n\n**Decision:** Yes, a user can be in any number of groups.\n\n**Reasoning:** The data model already requires a many-to-many join between users and groups. There is no scheduling conflict risk because a group booking is always checked against each member's individual limits before it is confirmed. Restricting this would hurt real use cases with no benefit.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** A per-user group limit if needed.\n\n---\n\n### 3. What do members see of each other?\n\n**Decision:** Free/busy only. No task titles, goal names, or estimates are visible to other members.\n\n**Reasoning:** Task details reveal what a person is studying and how far behind they are. That is sensitive. Free/busy is enough to compute common slots. Starting restrictive is easier to relax later than the reverse.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Optional sharing of task titles within a group, if users ask for it.\n\n---\n\n### 4. Does a group session count toward each member's block limits?\n\n**Decision:** Yes. A group booking counts as one block for every attending member, toward both the 8-block daily limit and the 40-block weekly limit.\n\n**Reasoning:** A group session is real focused time. Excluding it from limits would let users exceed burnout thresholds by filling their schedule with group sessions. The backend's limit checker must see a block row per member; it has no concept of \"group\" vs \"personal.\"\n\n**Implementation note:** When a group booking is confirmed, the backend creates one Block row per attending member. The GroupBooking row links them. Limit checks run before the booking is written.\n\n---\n\n### 5. Booking model — does everyone confirm, or does first booking win?\n\n**Decision:** First booking wins. The first member to book a free slot locks it for the group.\n\n**Reasoning:** A confirmation flow requires a pending state, a notification system, and timeout logic — significant complexity for v1. With 10 known users coordinating casually, first-booking is practical. The booking screen shows a clear confirmation step: \"Book this slot for the group?\" before the request is sent, so it is not accidental.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** All-must-confirm model, booking proposals, notifications.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Who can cancel a booking?\n\n**Decision:** Only the member who made the booking can cancel it. There is no edit flow — cancel and rebook instead.\n\n**Reasoning:** Allowing any member to cancel creates coordination problems (someone cancels without telling others). Only-the-booker is simpler and predictable. Concurrency — preventing two members booking the same slot simultaneously\n\n**Decision:** Use a database transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the affected rows. The availability check and the insert happen inside a single serializable transaction.\n\n**Reasoning:** Without a lock, two members could both pass the availability check at the same time and both write a booking, resulting in an overbooked slot. `SELECT FOR UPDATE` ensures only one transaction proceeds; the second reads the updated state and fails cleanly with a \"slot no longer available\" error, which the app surfaces to the user.\n\n**Implementation note:** This is a learning objective. The concurrency test in the testing plan (section 14 of the design doc) must cover this case explicitly: simulate two simultaneous booking requests for the same slot and assert that exactly one succeeds.\n\n---\n\n### 8. Block rows on booking\n\n**Decision:** Confirming a group booking creates one Block row per attending member. The GroupBooking row stores the group-level metadata and links to the individual block rows.\n\n**Reasoning:** The limit checker (daily and weekly block counts) only reads Block rows. If group bookings did not produce Block rows, the checker would be blind to them. This is the cleanest way to keep the limit logic simple and uniform — it does not need to know about groups at all.\n\n**Schema implication:**\n\n```\nGroupBooking\n  id\n  group_id\n  start\n  end\n  booked_by (user_id)\n  status\n\nBlock\n  id\n  task_id         -- NULL for a group booking block\n  group_booking_id -- NULL for a personal block; set for group booking blocks\n  user_id\n  start\n  end\n  actual_time_spent\n  status\n```\n\nOne of `task_id` or `group_booking_id` is set; the other is null. The limit checker counts all Block rows for a user regardless of which column is set.\n\n---\n\n### 9. Minimum group size\n\n**Decision:** A group must have at least 2 members before a booking can be made. A group can be created with 1 member (the creator), but the \"view free slots\" and \"book\" actions are disabled until a second member joins.\n\n**Reasoning:** A group session with one person is just a personal block. Enforcing the minimum on the booking action (not on creation) avoids blocking the natural flow of creating a group and then sharing the invite code.\n\n---\n\n### 10. Group free slots — computation, not storage\n\n**Decision:** Group free slots are always computed on demand and never stored.\n\n**Reasoning:** Consistent with the core principle in section 6 of the design doc: suggestions are never stored as facts. This must be enforced on the backend, not the client.\n\n---\n\n## What is not in v1 (Group)\n\n| Feature | Reason deferred |\n|---|---|\n| Approval-based joining | Async complexity |\n| All-must-confirm booking | Notification and state complexity |\n| Any-member cancel | Coordination risk, not worth the complexity |\n| Booking edit (change time) | Equivalent to cancel + rebook |\n| Task detail visibility | Privacy; free/busy is enough |\n| Invite expiry or revoke | Not needed for 10 known users |\n| Group size limit | Not needed for v1 scale |\n| Automatic group slot suggestions | Explicitly out of scope (design doc section 2) |\n\n---\n\n## Open questions resolved by these decisions\n\nAll open questions from section 11 of the design doc are now resolved for v1.\n\nThe only remaining group-related question is from section 18 (open questions): whether a group session counts toward limits. **Answered above: yes, it does.**\n",

                "summary": "Create decisions.md for the group feature of the Study Planner project",
                "file_text": "# Group Feature Decisions\n**Project:** Study Planner with Free-Slot Finder\n**Author:** Srividya\n**Date:** 22 October 2026\n**Status:** Decided — v1\n\n---\n\n## Context\n\nSection 11 of the design doc listed the group feature as partially open. This document records the final decisions for v1, the reasoning behind each, and what is explicitly deferred to v2.\n\n---\n\n## Decisions\n\n### 1. How groups are created and joined\n\n**Decision:** Invite code only.\n\nA group creator generates a short random code. Anyone with the code can join. No approval flow in v1.\n\n**Reasoning:** An approval flow requires async state (pending / accepted / rejected), extra API endpoints, and notification logic. For v1 with 10 known users, an invite code is sufficient. The data cost is one extra field on the Group table.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Approval-based joining, invite expiry, revoke invite.\n\n---\n\n### 2. Can a user be in multiple groups?\n\n**Decision:** Yes, a user can be in any number of groups.\n\n**Reasoning:** The data model already requires a many-to-many join between users and groups. There is no scheduling conflict risk because a group booking is always checked against each member's individual limits before it is confirmed. Restricting this would hurt real use cases with no benefit.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** A per-user group limit if needed.\n\n---\n\n### 3. What do members see of each other?\n\n**Decision:** Free/busy only. No task titles, goal names, or estimates are visible to other members.\n\n**Reasoning:** Task details reveal what a person is studying and how far behind they are. That is sensitive. Free/busy is enough to compute common slots. Starting restrictive is easier to relax later than the reverse.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** Optional sharing of task titles within a group, if users ask for it.\n\n---\n\n### 4. Does a group session count toward each member's block limits?\n\n**Decision:** Yes. A group booking counts as one block for every attending member, toward both the 8-block daily limit and the 40-block weekly limit.\n\n**Reasoning:** A group session is real focused time. Excluding it from limits would let users exceed burnout thresholds by filling their schedule with group sessions. The backend's limit checker must see a block row per member; it has no concept of \"group\" vs \"personal.\"\n\n**Implementation note:** When a group booking is confirmed, the backend creates one Block row per attending member. The GroupBooking row links them. Limit checks run before the booking is written.\n\n---\n\n### 5. Booking model — does everyone confirm, or does first booking win?\n\n**Decision:** First booking wins. The first member to book a free slot locks it for the group.\n\n**Reasoning:** A confirmation flow requires a pending state, a notification system, and timeout logic — significant complexity for v1. With 10 known users coordinating casually, first-booking is practical. The booking screen shows a clear confirmation step: \"Book this slot for the group?\" before the request is sent, so it is not accidental.\n\n**Deferred to v2:** All-must-confirm model, booking proposals, notifications.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Who can cancel a booking?\n\n**Decision:** Only the member who made the booking can cancel it. This is a permanent rule, not a v1 limitation. There is no edit flow — cancel and rebook instead.\n\n**Reasoning:** Allowing any member to cancel creates coordination problems (someone cancels without telling others). Only-the-booker is simpler and predictable. An edit flow (change the time) requires re-running availability checks for all members and is equivalent to cancel-and-rebook anyway, so it is not worth building.\n\n---\n\n### 7. Concurrency — preventing two members booking the same slot simultaneously\n\n**Decision:** Use a database transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the affected rows. The availability check and the insert happen inside a single serializable transaction.\n\n**Reasoning:** Without a lock, two members could both pass the availability check at the same time and both write a booking, resulting in an overbooked slot. `SELECT FOR UPDATE` ensures only one transaction proceeds; the second reads the updated state and fails cleanly with a \"slot no longer available\" error, which the app surfaces to the user.\n\n**Implementation note:** This is a learning objective. The concurrency test in the testing plan (section 14 of the design doc) must cover this case explicitly: simulate two simultaneous booking requests for the same slot and assert that exactly one succeeds.\n\n---\n\n### 8. Block rows on booking\n\n**Decision:** Confirming a group booking creates one Block row per attending member. The GroupBooking row stores the group-level metadata and links to the individual Block rows.\n\n**Reasoning:** The limit checker (daily and weekly block counts) only reads Block rows. If group bookings did not produce Block rows, the checker would be blind to them. This keeps the limit logic simple and uniform — it does not need to know about groups at all.\n\n**Schema implication:**\n\n```\nGroupBooking\n  id\n  group_id\n  start\n  end\n  booked_by (user_id)\n  status\n\nBlock\n  id\n  task_id          -- NULL for a group booking block\n  group_booking_id -- NULL for a personal block; set for group booking blocks\n  user_id\n  start\n  end\n  actual_time_spent\n  status\n```\n\nOne of `task_id` or `group_booking_id` is set; the other is null. The limit checker counts all Block rows for a user regardless of which column is set.\n\n---\n\n### 9. Minimum group size\n\n**Decision:** A group must have at least 2 members before a booking can be made. A group can be created with 1 member (the creator), but the \"view free slots\" and \"book\" actions are disabled until a second member joins.\n\n**Reasoning:** A group session with one person is just a personal block. Enforcing the minimum on the booking action (not on creation) avoids blocking the natural flow of creating a group and then sharing the invite code.\n\n---\n\n### 10. Group free slots — computation, not storage\n\n**Decision:** Group free slots are always computed on demand and never stored.\n\n**Reasoning:** Consistent with the core principle in section 6 of the design doc: suggestions are never stored as facts. A group free slot is the intersection of all members' free intervals, filtered to times where every member has capacity under their limits. This result changes whenever any member's schedule changes, so caching it would require invalidation logic that is not worth building in v1.\n\n**Algorithm note:** The group free-slot computation is a generalisation of the personal free-slot computation. Given N members, intersect their free intervals pairwise, then filter the result to slots of at least 65 minutes (50-minute block + 15-minute gap minimum). This belongs in the scheduler module (pure logic, no database or API dependencies) alongside the personal slot finder.\n\n**API note:** `GET /groups/{id}/free-slots` is accessible only to members of that group. A non-member receives 403. This must be enforced on the backend, not the client.\n\n---\n\n## What is not in v1 (Group)\n\n| Feature | Reason deferred |\n|---|---|\n| Approval-based joining | Async complexity |\n| All-must-confirm booking | Notification and state complexity |\n| Booking edit (change time) | Equivalent to cancel + rebook |\n| Task detail visibility | Privacy; free/busy is enough |\n| Invite expiry or revoke | Not needed for 10 known users |\n| Group size limit | Not needed for v1 scale |\n| Automatic group slot suggestions | Explicitly out of scope (design doc section 2) |\n\n---\n\n## Permanently out of scope (any version)\n\n| Feature | Reason |\n|---|---|\n| Any member can cancel a booking | Only the booker can cancel; this is a permanent design decision, not a v1 limitation |\n\n---\n\n## Open questions resolved by these decisions\n\nAll open questions from section 11 of the design doc are now resolved.\n\nThe only remaining group-related item from section 18 (open questions) was whether a group session counts toward limits. **Answered: yes, it does.**\n"
              },

Before I give a recommendation, let me ask a few quick questions so the advice is actually useful for you:\n\n**1. What's your current experience level?**\nHave you used any backend language before (Python, Java, Node, anything)? Or is this genuinely starting from zero?\n\n**2. What's the primary learning goal for the backend?**\nThe doc lists: REST APIs, auth, relational databases, interval algorithms, date/time handling, concurrency, testing, deployment. Is there one you care most about, or is it all roughly equal?\n\n**3. Flutter is already decided, right?**\nThe doc reads like Flutter is fixed. Is that confirmed, or is the frontend also open?\n\n**4. Timeline pressure?**\nIs there a deadline (semester project, internship, etc.) or is this self-paced?\n\n---\n\nWhile you answer, here's the honest shape of the decision:\n\n**Go** is genuinely excellent for this project — strong concurrency primitives (useful for the double-booking problem), fast, and the standard library covers most of what you need. The tradeoff is that Go is strict and verbose, so the learning curve at the start is steeper. You'll write more code before anything works.\n\n**PostgreSQL** is the right database regardless of what language you pick. For a relational, rules-heavy scheduler with transactions and interval math, it's the clear choice. No debate there.\n\nThe real question is whether Go is the right language *for you* at this stage, or whether something like Python (FastAPI) or Node (with TypeScript) would get you to the interesting parts — the scheduler logic, concurrency, deployment — faster without fighting the language itself.\n\nTell me where you're starting from and we can settle it."

          "content": "Starting from zero, no deadline, Flutter decided, all learning goals equal weight. That's actually the clearest possible situation — pick what teaches the most transferable skills, not what's fastest.\n\nHere's my honest take:\n\n---\n\n## Backend Language\n\n**Go is the right choice. Stick with it.**\n\nHere's why it fits this specific project better than the alternatives:\n\n- The scheduler is pure logic with no side effects. Go's simplicity (no classes, no magic, explicit everything) is actually an advantage here — you'll write the interval logic in plain functions and it'll be easy to test in isolation, exactly what section 8 asks for.\n- The concurrency chapter (double-booking prevention) maps directly to things Go was designed for. You'll learn goroutines and understand why `SELECT FOR UPDATE` is necessary at the database level rather than trying to handle it in the language. That's a deeper lesson than most frameworks give you.\n- Go forces you to handle errors explicitly. That sounds annoying, but for a project where every rejected action needs a clear reason (your own requirement), it builds the right habits.\n- The REST API layer in Go is straightforward with the standard library alone. You don't need a framework to start.\n- What you learn in Go transfers directly to systems thinking, which is more durable than framework-specific knowledge.\n\n**The tradeoff:** The first two weeks will be slow. Go is strict about types, unused imports, and error handling. Push through that phase — it gets fast after.\n\n---\n\n## Database\n\n**PostgreSQL. No debate.** Already covered — transactions, interval types, constraints, everything this project needs is native.\n\n---\n\n## Flutter\n\nAlready decided. One thing to confirm now rather than later: pick **one state management approach before you write a single screen**. The doc lists it as something to decide. The right choice for a learning project at this scale is **Provider** — it's simple, well-documented, and used widely enough that every problem you hit has a Stack Overflow answer. Riverpod and Bloc are better for larger apps but add abstraction you don't need yet.\n\n---\n\n## Full Stack Summary\n\n| Layer | Choice | Status |\n|---|---|---|\n| Mobile | Flutter + Dart | Confirmed |\n| State management | Provider | Decide now |\n| Backend | Go | Confirm |\n| Database | PostgreSQL | Confirm |\n| Auth | JWT (stateless, fits REST) | Standard choice |\n| Hosting | Single VPS (Railway or Render for learning) | Decide at milestone 7 |\n\n---\n\nTwo things to confirm right now so the design doc can be updated:\n1. Go confirmed as backend language?\n2. Provider confirmed as Flutter state management?"
        }

          "content": "This changes the answer. Job market matters, and you're right to flag it.\n\nLet me be straight with you.\n\n---\n\n## The honest job market picture (India, 2026)\n\n**MERN (MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js)** is the most commonly listed stack in entry-level and internship job postings in India. Recruiters recognise it by name. Your resume saying \"MERN stack\" gets parsed faster by non-technical HR screens.\n\n**Go + Flutter** is a strong stack but it's a specialist stack. Companies that use Go are usually product companies, startups at scale, or infra teams. They exist, they pay well, but there are fewer entry-level openings compared to MERN/full-stack web roles.\n\n**Flutter specifically** is a mobile-only skill. If your goal is to become a general developer and get hired, Flutter narrows your options. Web developers are hired far more broadly than mobile developers at the entry level in India.\n\n---\n\n## The real question\n\nWhat kind of developer do you want to be?\n\n- **Web developer (frontend + backend):** MERN is the right stack. React is everywhere. Node/Express is learnable fast. MongoDB works for simple projects though it has real tradeoffs.\n- **Mobile developer:** Flutter + Dart, but know this is a narrower market.\n- **Backend/systems developer:** Go or Java Spring Boot. Fewer jobs but higher quality ones.\n\n---\n\n## My recommendation for a student looking for jobs\n\n**Switch the stack to MERN, but keep PostgreSQL instead of MongoDB.**\n\nHere is why:\n\nReact + Node.js + Express are on almost every job description. Learning them on this project means every feature you build is also portfolio evidence of industry-relevant skills.\n\nMongoDB is the default in MERN but it is genuinely the wrong database for this project. Your scheduler has hard relational constraints, transactions, and interval logic. MongoDB will fight you at every step. PostgreSQL with Node.js (using a library like `pg` or Prisma) is better technically and also teaches you SQL, which every job expects regardless of stack.\n\nSo: **React Native or React (web) + Node.js + Express + PostgreSQL.**\n\nOne more decision: **React Native vs Flutter.**\n- If you want mobile only: Flutter is fine but narrow. React Native uses JavaScript which you'll already know from React, so the skill transfers.\n- If you are open to building this as a web app instead: drop mobile entirely, use React for the frontend. Web apps are easier to deploy, easier to demo, and more relevant to most job descriptions.\n\n---\n\n## My actual suggestion\n\nBuild this as a **web app**, not a mobile app.\n\nStack: **React + Node.js + Express + PostgreSQL**\n\nReasons:\n- Every skill transfers directly to job requirements\n- Easier to deploy and share (just a URL, no APK)\n- React is the most demanded frontend skill in India by a large margin\n- Node.js means one language (JavaScript) across frontend and backend, which reduces cognitive load while learning\n- PostgreSQL teaches you real SQL and relational thinking, which is valued everywhere\n- The scheduler logic, REST API, auth, concurrency — everything in your learning plan still applies exactly\n\nThe only thing you lose is Flutter. And Flutter, for a job-seeking student targeting the broad developer market, is the weakest part of your original stack.\n\n---\n\n## Decision table\n\n| Layer | Original | Recommended | Why |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Frontend | Flutter | React (web) | Most hired skill, transfers everywhere |\n| Backend | Go | Node.js + Express | Same language as frontend, huge job market |\n| Database | PostgreSQL | PostgreSQL | Keep this, it's the right call |\n| Auth | JWT | JWT | Same |\n| State mgmt | Provider | React Context or Zustand | Simple, learnable |\n\n---\n\nYour call. But if I were advising a student who wants to get hired: **React + Node + PostgreSQL, built as a web app.** Everything in your design doc still holds — the scheduler, the rules, the groups, the burnout limits — none of that changes. Only the frontend technology changes.\n\nWhat do you want to do?"

            "prompt": "lets do onthing lets make two branch one follows mern and other follows go+flutter so that i can learn both one after other "

          "message_id": "2fafa4dd-a1b0-4f47-b622-021d2d8780bd",
          "content": "That's actually a smart approach. Build the project twice — same problem domain, different stack. The second time will go much faster because you already know the domain deeply.\n\nBut let me flag one thing before we plan this:\n\n**Build them sequentially, not in parallel.** If you try to maintain two branches simultaneously, you'll context-switch constantly and learn neither well. Finish one completely, deploy it, then start the second.\n\n---\n\n## The plan\n\n**Branch 1 — Web first (MERN-ish)**\nStack: React + Node.js + Express + PostgreSQL\nWhy first: JavaScript across the stack reduces friction while you're learning the domain. You'll make mistakes on the scheduler logic, the auth flow, the group booking — better to make them in the forgiving stack first.\n\n**Branch 2 — Go + Flutter**\nWhy second: By the time you start this, you know the domain cold. You know exactly what the API needs to do, what the database schema looks like, what edge cases exist. You can focus entirely on learning Go and Flutter without also figuring out the product.\n\n---\n\n## Git structure\n\n```\nmain\n├── branch: mern         ← build this first, fully\n└── branch: go-flutter   ← start this after mern is deployed\n```\n\nKeep `main` as the design doc and decisions only — no code. Each branch is a self-contained project.\n\n---\n\n## What stays the same across both branches\n\nEverything in your design doc. The rules, the scheduler logic, the data model, the API shape, the group feature decisions — all of it. The problem doesn't change, only the tools.\n\nThis also means your `decisions.md` applies to both branches. You only need to write the design once.\n\n---\n\n## Updated tech stack table\n\n| Layer | Branch: mern | Branch: go-flutter |\n|---|---|---|\n| Frontend | React (web) | Flutter (mobile) |\n| Backend | Node.js + Express | Go |\n| Database | PostgreSQL | PostgreSQL |\n| Auth | JWT | JWT |\n| State management | Zustand | Provider |\n| ORM / DB layer | Prisma | pgx (raw) |\n\nPostgreSQL is the same in both. That's intentional — you learn the database once, deeply.\n\n---\n\nShould I update the design doc and decisions.md to reflect this two-branch plan, and add a `techstack.md` that documents both?"
        }
      },

                "file_text": "# Tech Stack & Learning Plan\n**Project:** Study Planner with Free-Slot Finder\n**Author:** Srividya\n**Date:** 22 October 2026\n**Status:** Decided\n\n---\n\n## Overview\n\nThis project is built twice, on two separate branches. The problem, the rules, the data model, and the API shape are identical across both. Only the tools change. The goal is to learn two industry-relevant stacks on the same well-understood domain.\n\nBuild them **sequentially, not in parallel.** Finish and deploy Branch 1 completely before starting Branch 2.\n\n---\n\n## Branch 1 — MERN (build first)\n\n**`branch: mern`**\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Frontend | React (web app) |\n| Backend | Node.js + Express |\n| Database | PostgreSQL |\n| Auth | JWT |\n| State management | Zustand |\n| DB layer | Prisma |\n\n### Why this branch is first\n\nJavaScript runs on both the frontend and the backend. While learning the domain — the scheduler logic, the auth flow, the group booking, the burnout rules — using one language across the stack removes one source of friction. You will make mistakes on the product. Better to make them here.\n\nReact is the most demanded frontend skill in entry-level and internship job postings in India. Node.js + Express is widely listed alongside it. Finishing this branch gives you a deployable web app and a resume entry that recruiters recognise by name.\n\n### Why PostgreSQL and not MongoDB\n\nMongoDB is the default M in MERN but it is the wrong database for this project. The scheduler has hard relational constraints, transactions, interval logic, and strict limit enforcement. These are relational problems. PostgreSQL handles them natively. MongoDB would require workarounds at every step.\n\nUsing PostgreSQL here also means you learn SQL once, deeply, and carry that knowledge into Branch 2 without relearning anything.\n\n### Why Prisma\n\nPrisma is a Node.js ORM that generates a type-safe client from your schema. For a learning project it makes the database layer readable and catches mistakes early. It also handles migrations cleanly.\n\n### What you learn in this branch\n\n- JavaScript (Node.js and browser)\n- React: components, hooks, forms, routing, API calls, timeline view\n- Zustand: simple state management\n- Express: routing, middleware, validation, error handling\n- REST API design: resources, status codes, clear error messages\n- JWT auth: signup, login, protected routes\n- PostgreSQL: schema design, queries, transactions, constraints\n- Prisma: schema definition, migrations, queries\n- Interval algorithms and date/time handling in JavaScript\n- Concurrency: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction\n- Testing: Jest for unit tests, Supertest for API tests\n- Deployment: Node server + PostgreSQL on a VPS or platform\n\n---\n\n## Branch 2 — Go + Flutter (build second)\n\n**`branch: go-flutter`**\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Frontend | Flutter (Android app) |\n| Backend | Go |\n| Database | PostgreSQL |\n| Auth | JWT |\n| State management | Provider |\n| DB layer | pgx (raw queries) |\n\n### Why this branch is second\n\nBy the time you start this branch, you know the domain completely. You know exactly what the API must do, what the database schema looks like, and where the edge cases are. The scheduler logic is already written and tested. You can focus entirely on learning Go and Flutter without also figuring out the product.\n\nGo is a strong backend language for companies that need performance and correctness — product startups, infra teams, fintech. It is a specialist skill that pays well. Flutter is the leading cross-platform mobile framework. Together they represent a different and complementary part of the job market.\n\n### Why pgx and not an ORM\n\nGo developers typically write raw SQL. pgx is the standard PostgreSQL driver for Go. Writing queries by hand in this branch teaches you SQL at a deeper level and reflects what you will actually do in Go jobs. The schema is already designed from Branch 1, so this is not extra design work.\n\n### What you learn in this branch\n\n- Go: types, interfaces, error handling, structs, packages\n- Go standard library: HTTP server, JSON, time\n- Go concurrency primitives: goroutines, channels (background for the double-booking lesson)\n- Flutter: widgets, navigation, forms, API calls, timeline view\n- Dart: language basics\n- Provider: state management in Flutter\n- Pure function design: the scheduler as isolated, testable logic\n- pgx: connecting to PostgreSQL, running queries, transactions\n- JWT in Go\n- Testing in Go: table-driven unit tests for the scheduler\n- Deployment: Go binary + PostgreSQL, build an Android APK\n\n---\n\n## What is the same in both branches\n\nEverything in the design doc and decisions.md applies to both branches without change.\n\n| Thing | Same? |\n|---|---|\n| All scheduling rules | Yes |\n| Burnout limits (8/day, 40/week) | Yes |\n| Block and gap lengths | Yes |\n| Data model and entities | Yes |\n| API resources and shape | Yes |\n| Group feature decisions | Yes |\n| JWT auth | Yes |\n| PostgreSQL schema | Yes (same schema, same migrations logic) |\n| Scheduler as pure logic, separate from DB and API | Yes |\n| Backend is source of truth | Yes |\n| Suggestions never stored | Yes |\n\n---\n\n## Git structure\n\n```\nmain                  ← design docs only, no code\n├── mern              ← Branch 1, built first\n└── go-flutter        ← Branch 2, built after mern is deployed\n```\n\n`main` holds:\n- `decisions.md`\n- `techstack.md`\n- `design-doc.md` (when written up)\n\nNo application code lives on `main`.\n\n---\n\n## Sequence\n\n1. Complete Branch 1 (mern) through all 7 milestones in the learning plan.\n2. Deploy Branch 1. Test with real users.\n3. Then start Branch 2 (go-flutter) from milestone 1.\n4. Deploy Branch 2. Compare what felt different.\n\nDo not switch between branches mid-milestone. Finish what you started.\n\n---\n\n## Resume impact\n\nAfter Branch 1: React, Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, REST APIs, JWT, Zustand, Prisma, Jest, deployment. Covers most entry-level full-stack web job requirements in India.\n\nAfter Branch 2: Go, Flutter, Dart, pgx, Provider, Android APK build. Adds mobile and systems backend skills. Differentiates your resume from the typical MERN-only candidate.\n\nBoth together: you have built the same non-trivial product twice, in two different stacks, with tests and deployment. That is a strong portfolio story.\n",
                "summary": "Create techstack.md documenting the two-branch learning strategy"

For a learning project it makes the database layer readable and catches mistakes early. It also handles migrations cleanly.\n\n### What you learn in this branch\n\n- JavaScript (Node.js and browser)\n- React: components, hooks, forms, routing, API calls, timeline view\n- Zustand: simple state management\n- Express: routing, middleware, validation, error handling\n- REST API design: resources, status codes, clear error messages\n- JWT auth: signup, login, protected routes\n- PostgreSQL: schema design, queries, transactions, constraints\n- Prisma: schema definition, migrations, queries\n- Interval algorithms and date/time handling in JavaScript\n- Concurrency: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction\n- Testing: Jest for unit tests, Supertest for API tests\n- Deployment: Node server + PostgreSQL on a VPS or platform\n\n---\n\n## Branch 2 — Go + Flutter (build second)\n\n**`branch: go-flutter`**\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Frontend | Flutter (Android app) |\n| Backend | Go |\n| Database | PostgreSQL |\n| Auth | JWT |\n| State management | Provider |\n| DB layer | pgx (raw queries) |\n\n### Why this branch is second\n\nBy the time you start this branch, you know the domain completely. You know exactly what the API must do, what the database schema looks like, and where the edge cases are. The scheduler logic is already written and tested. You can focus entirely on learning Go and Flutter without also figuring out the product.\n\nGo is a strong backend language for companies that need performance and correctness — product startups, infra teams, fintech. It is a specialist skill that pays well. Flutter is the leading cross-platform mobile framework. Together they represent a different and complementary part of the job market.\n\n### Why pgx and not an ORM\n\nGo developers typically write raw SQL. pgx is the standard PostgreSQL driver for Go. Writing queries by hand in this branch teaches you SQL at a deeper level and reflects what you will actually do in Go jobs. The schema is already designed from Branch 1, so this is not extra design work.\n\n### What you learn in this branch\n\n- Go: types, interfaces, error handling, structs, packages\n- Go standard library: HTTP server, JSON, time\n- Go concurrency primitives: goroutines, channels (background for the double-booking lesson)\n- Flutter: widgets, navigation, forms, API calls, timeline view\n- Dart: language basics\n- Provider: state management in Flutter\n- Pure function design: the scheduler as isolated, testable logic\n- pgx: connecting to PostgreSQL, running queries, transactions\n- JWT in Go\n- Testing in Go: table-driven unit tests for the scheduler\n- Deployment: Go binary + PostgreSQL, build an Android APK\n\n---\n\n## What is the same in both branches\n\nEverything in the design doc and decisions.md applies to both branches without change.\n\n| Thing | Same? |\n|---|---|\n| All scheduling rules | Yes |\n| Burnout limits (8/day, 40/week) | Yes |\n| Block and gap lengths | Yes |\n| Data model and entities | Yes |\n| API resources and shape | Yes |\n| Group feature decisions | Yes |\n| JWT auth | Yes |\n| PostgreSQL schema | Yes (same schema, same migrations logic) |\n| Scheduler as pure logic, separate from DB and API | Yes |\n| Backend is source of truth | Yes |\n| Suggestions never stored | Yes |\n\n---\n\n## Git structure\n\n```\nmain                  ← design docs only, no code\n├── mern              ← Branch 1, built first\n└── go-flutter        ← Branch 2, built after mern is deployed\n```\n\n`main` holds:\n- `decisions.md`\n- `techstack.md`\n- `design-doc.md` (when written up)\n\nNo application code lives on `main`.\n\n---\n\n## Sequence\n\n1. Complete Branch 1 (mern) through all 7 milestones in the learning plan.\n2. Deploy Branch 1. Test with real users.\n3. Then start Branch 2 (go-flutter) from milestone 1.\n4. Deploy Branch 2. Compare what felt different.\n\nDo not switch between branches mid-milestone. Finish what you started.\n\n---\n\n## Resume impact\n\nAfter Branch 1: React, Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, REST APIs, JWT, Zustand, Prisma, Jest, deployment. Covers most entry-level full-stack web job requirements in India.\n\nAfter Branch 2: Go, Flutter, Dart, pgx, Provider, Android APK build. Adds mobile and systems backend skills. Differentiates your resume from the typical MERN-only candidate.\n\nBoth together: you have built the same non-trivial product twice, in two different stacks, with tests and deployment. That is a strong portfolio story.\n",
                "summary": "Create techstack.md documenting the two-branch learning strategy"
              }
            }
          ]
        }

                "file_text": "# Tech Stack & Learning Plan\n**Project:** Study Planner with Free-Slot Finder\n**Author:** Srividya\n**Date:** 22 October 2026\n**Status:** Decided\n\n---\n\n## Overview\n\nThis project is built twice, on two separate branches. The problem, the rules, the data model, and the API shape are identical across both. Only the tools change. The goal is to learn two industry-relevant stacks on the same well-understood domain.\n\nBuild them **sequentially, not in parallel.** Finish and deploy Branch 1 completely before starting Branch 2.\n\n---\n\n## Branch 1 — MERN (build first)\n\n**`branch: mern`**\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Frontend | React (web app) |\n| Backend | Node.js + Express |\n| Database | PostgreSQL |\n| Auth | JWT |\n| State management | Zustand |\n| DB layer | Prisma |\n\n### Why this branch is first\n\nJavaScript runs on both the frontend and the backend. While learning the domain — the scheduler logic, the auth flow, the group booking, the burnout rules — using one language across the stack removes one source of friction. You will make mistakes on the product. Better to make them here.\n\nReact is the most demanded frontend skill in entry-level and internship job postings in India. Node.js + Express is widely listed alongside it. Finishing this branch gives you a deployable web app and a resume entry that recruiters recognise by name.\n\n### Why PostgreSQL and not MongoDB\n\nMongoDB is the default M in MERN but it is the wrong database for this project. The scheduler has hard relational constraints, transactions, interval logic, and strict limit enforcement. These are relational problems. PostgreSQL handles them natively. MongoDB would require workarounds at every step.\n\nUsing PostgreSQL here also means you learn SQL once, deeply, and carry that knowledge into Branch 2 without relearning anything.\n\n### Why Prisma\n\nPrisma is a Node.js ORM that generates a type-safe client from your schema. For a learning project it makes the database layer readable and catches mistakes early. It also handles migrations cleanly.\n\n### What you learn in this branch\n\n- JavaScript (Node.js and browser)\n- React: components, hooks, forms, routing, API calls, timeline view\n- Zustand: simple state management\n- Express: routing, middleware, validation, error handling\n- REST API design: resources, status codes, clear error messages\n- JWT auth: signup, login, protected routes\n- PostgreSQL: schema design, queries, transactions, constraints\n- Prisma: schema definition, migrations, queries\n- Interval algorithms and date/time handling in JavaScript\n- Concurrency: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction\n- Testing: Jest for unit tests, Supertest for API tests\n- Deployment: Node server + PostgreSQL on a VPS or platform\n\n---\n\n## Branch 2 — Go + Flutter (build second)\n\n**`branch: go-flutter`**\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Frontend | Flutter (Android app) |\n| Backend | Go |\n| Database | PostgreSQL |\n| Auth | JWT |\n| State management | Provider |\n| DB layer | pgx (raw queries) |\n\n### Why this branch is second\n\nBy the time you start this branch, you know the domain completely. You know exactly what the API must do, what the database schema looks like, and where the edge cases are. The scheduler logic is already written and tested. You can focus entirely on learning Go and Flutter without also figuring out the product.\n\nGo is a strong backend language for companies that need performance and correctness — product startups, infra teams, fintech. It is a specialist skill that pays well. Flutter is the leading cross-platform mobile framework. Together they represent a different and complementary part of the job market.\n\n### Why pgx and not an ORM\n\nGo developers typically write raw SQL. pgx is the standard PostgreSQL driver for Go. Writing queries by hand in this branch teaches you SQL at a deeper level and reflects what you will actually do in Go jobs. The schema is already designed from Branch 1, so this is not extra design work.\n\n### What you learn in this branch\n\n- Go: types, interfaces, error handling, structs, packages\n- Go standard library: HTTP server, JSON, time\n- Go concurrency primitives: goroutines, channels (background for the double-booking lesson)\n- Flutter: widgets, navigation, forms, API calls, timeline view\n- Dart: language basics\n- Provider: state management in Flutter\n- Pure function design: the scheduler as isolated, testable logic\n- pgx: connecting to PostgreSQL, running queries, transactions\n- JWT in Go\n- Testing in Go: table-driven unit tests for the scheduler\n- Deployment: Go binary + PostgreSQL, build an Android APK\n\n---\n\n## What is the same in both branches\n\nEverything in the design doc and decisions.md applies to both branches without change.\n\n| Thing | Same? |\n|---|---|\n| All scheduling rules | Yes |\n| Burnout limits (8/day, 40/week) | Yes |\n| Block and gap lengths | Yes |\n| Data model and entities | Yes |\n| API resources and shape | Yes |\n| Group feature decisions | Yes |\n| JWT auth | Yes |\n| PostgreSQL schema | Yes (same schema, same migrations logic) |\n| Scheduler as pure logic, separate from DB and API | Yes |\n| Backend is source of truth | Yes |\n| Suggestions never stored | Yes |\n\n---\n\n## Git structure\n\n```\nmain                  ← design docs only, no code\n├── mern              ← Branch 1, built first\n└── go-flutter        ← Branch 2, built after mern is deployed\n```\n\n`main` holds:\n- `decisions.md`\n- `techstack.md`\n- `design-doc.md` (when written up)\n\nNo application code lives on `main`.\n\n---\n\n## Sequence\n\n1. Complete Branch 1 (mern) through all 7 milestones in the learning plan.\n2. Deploy Branch 1. Test with real users.\n3. Then start Branch 2 (go-flutter) from milestone 1.\n4. Deploy Branch 2. Compare what felt different.\n\nDo not switch between branches mid-milestone. Finish what you started.\n\n---\n\n## Resume impact\n\nAfter Branch 1: React, Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, REST APIs, JWT, Zustand, Prisma, Jest, deployment. Covers most entry-level full-stack web job requirements in India.\n\nAfter Branch 2: Go, Flutter, Dart, pgx, Provider, Android APK build. Adds mobile and systems backend skills. Differentiates your resume from the typical MERN-only candidate.\n\nBoth together: you have built the same non-trivial product twice, in two different stacks, with tests and deployment. That is a strong portfolio story.\n",
                "summary": "Create techstack.md documenting the two-branch learning strategy"

          "content": "Let's go through them one by one. Starting with the open questions since the schema depends on some of those answers.\n\n---\n\n## Section 18 Open Questions — Let's close them\n\nI'll go through each one. Some I can recommend directly, some need your input.\n\n---\n\n**Q1. Confirm Go and PostgreSQL.**\nAnswered in techstack.md. Go + PostgreSQL for Branch 2, Node + PostgreSQL for Branch 1. Closed.\n\n---\n\n**Q2. How do weights and ranks combine?**\n\nHere's a concrete formula proposal:\n\n```\npriority_score = (goal_weight × 0.5) + (goal_rank_score × 0.3) + (deadline_urgency × 0.2)\n```\n\n- `goal_weight` — a number the user sets, e.g. 1 to 5. Normalise to 0–1 by dividing by 5.\n- `goal_rank_score` — if user ranks goals 1st, 2nd, 3rd, convert to a score: `(total_goals - rank + 1) / total_goals`. So rank 1 of 3 goals = 3/3 = 1.0, rank 3 = 1/3 = 0.33.\n- `deadline_urgency` — `1 / days_until_deadline`, capped at 1. A task due today = 1.0, due in 10 days = 0.1.\n\nHigher score = suggested first. Ties broken by deadline (earlier deadline wins), then by task creation time (older task wins).\n\nDo you want to go with this or adjust the weights (0.5 / 0.3 / 0.2)?\n\n---\n\n**Q3. Which repeat patterns are in v1, and how are they stored?**\n\nProposed v1 patterns — keep it small:\n- None (one-time)\n- Daily\n- Weekly (same day each week)\n- Weekdays only (Mon–Fri)\n\nStorage: store as a string enum on the task row — `none`, `daily`, `weekly`, `weekdays`. Store the original task as the \"template.\" Each scheduled occurrence is a separate Block row. Do not generate infinite rows — generate only for the current week on demand.\n\nDoes this cover your real use cases, or do you need anything else like \"every 2 weeks\"?\n\n---\n\n**Q4. Time rules — smallest unit, UTC vs IST, week start.**\n\nProposals:\n- Smallest time unit: **5 minutes.** Slots snap to 5-minute boundaries (e.g. 9:00, 9:05). Simple and clean.\n- Storage: **store all times as UTC in the database.** Display in IST in the app. One conversion point, no ambiguity. IST is UTC+5:30, no DST, so the conversion is always the same fixed offset.\n- Week start: **Monday.** Standard for academic schedules. The 40-block weekly limit resets every Monday 00:00 IST.\n\nAgree with these?\n\n---\n\n**Q5. How are classes entered?**\n\nProposal: one entry form, two options the user picks — \"one-time\" or \"weekly (repeats every week on this day and time).\" That covers 95% of college schedules. No other repeat options for fixed events in v1.\n\n---\n\n**Q6. Gap rule.**\n\nProposal to confirm: **15 minutes after any block under 60 minutes, 25 minutes after a 60-minute block or after the third consecutive block.** This is what the doc already floated. Agree?\n\n---\n\n**Q7. Extra burnout rules — meal windows, end-of-day cutoff, rest day.**\n\nThese need your input:\n\n- **Meal windows:** Should the app block scheduling during lunch and dinner? Proposed: block 13:00–14:00 (lunch) and 20:00–21:00 (dinner) by default, user can change in settings.\n- **End-of-day cutoff:** No blocks after what time? Proposed: 22:00 IST by default, user can change.\n- **Rest day:** Should Sunday be a no-schedule day by default? Or leave it open and let the user decide?\n\nWhat feels right to you?\n\n---\n\n**Q8. Exact scoring formula.**\nCovered in Q2 above.\n\n---\n\nOnce you answer Q2, Q3, Q6, and Q7 above, all 18 open questions are closed and we can move straight to the schema and Git setup."

          "content": "Good calls. Let me address Q2 properly first.\n\n---\n\n## Q2 — Finding better weights\n\nThe formula shape is right. The question is what the three weights (w1, w2, w3) should be where w1 + w2 + w3 = 1.\n\nRather than guessing, let's reason from what the app actually cares about:\n\n**What matters most to a student?**\n- Missing a deadline is the worst outcome. Urgency should dominate.\n- Goal weight reflects how much the student cares about a subject. That's their own stated priority — it should matter a lot.\n- Goal rank is a tiebreaker within similar-weight goals. It's the weakest signal of the three.\n\n**Test cases to validate any formula:**\n\n| Scenario | Expected winner |\n|---|---|\n| Task A: high urgency, low goal weight vs Task B: low urgency, high goal weight | A should win — deadline pressure beats preference |\n| Task A: same urgency, high weight goal vs Task B: same urgency, low weight goal | A should win — goal weight is the differentiator |\n| Task A: same urgency, same weight, rank 1 goal vs Task B: rank 2 goal | A should win — rank breaks the tie |\n| Task A: deadline today, any goal vs Task B: deadline in 1 day, any goal | A should win clearly |\n\n**Three candidate weight sets to test:**\n\n| Set | Urgency | Goal weight | Goal rank | Reasoning |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| A | 0.5 | 0.35 | 0.15 | Urgency dominates strongly |\n| B | 0.4 | 0.4 | 0.2 | Urgency and goal weight equal |\n| C | 0.45 | 0.35 | 0.2 | Balanced, slight urgency lean |\n\nRun all three against your test cases when you build the scheduler. Pick the one that produces the most sensible suggestions across all scenarios. This is exactly the kind of thing you validate with unit tests — write the test cases above as actual test inputs and assert the expected winner.\n\n**Recommended default to start with: Set A (0.5 / 0.35 / 0.15).** Urgency should dominate for a student with deadlines. Adjust after testing.\n\n---\n\n## Q7 — Burnout rules with defaults (12-hour format)\n\n| Rule | Default | User can change? |\n|---|---|---|\n| Lunch block | 1:00 PM – 2:00 PM | Yes |\n| Dinner block | 8:00 PM – 9:00 PM | Yes |\n| End-of-day cutoff | No blocks after 10:00 PM | Yes |\n| Rest day | Sunday (no blocks scheduled) | Yes |\n\nAll four are stored in user settings, not hardcoded. The backend enforces whatever the user has set. If a user changes the lunch window to 12:30 PM – 1:30 PM, the scheduler respects that from the next suggestion onward.\n\n---\n\n## All open questions — final status\n\n| # | Question | Answer |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Confirm Go and PostgreSQL | Confirmed for Branch 2, Node + PostgreSQL for Branch 1 |\n| 2 | How do weights and ranks combine | Formula decided, start with Set A (0.5 / 0.35 / 0.15), validate with tests |\n| 3 | Repeat patterns and storage | none, daily, weekly, weekdays — stored as enum, generate per week on demand |\n| 4 | Time rules | 5-minute unit, store UTC display IST (UTC+5:30), week starts Monday |\n| 5 | How are classes entered | One-time or weekly, user picks |\n| 6 | Gap rule | 15 min after any block, 25 min after 60-min block or third consecutive block |\n| 7 | Burnout rules | Lunch 1–2 PM, Dinner 8–9 PM, cutoff 10 PM, Sunday rest — all defaults, all changeable |\n| 8 | Scoring formula | Same as Q2 |\n| 9 | All group rules | Closed in decisions.md |\n\n**All 18 open questions are now closed.**\n\n---\n\nReady to move to the schema and Git setup? I'd suggest doing them in this order:\n1. Write the full database schema (same for both branches)\n2. Document it in `schema.md`\n3. Set up the Git repo with the branch structure\n\nSay the word and I'll start on the schema."

                "file_text": "# Open Questions — Decisions & Scoring Formula\n**Project:** Study Planner with Free-Slot Finder\n**Author:** Srividya\n**Date:** 22 October 2026\n**Status:** Decided — v1\n\n---\n\n## Overview\n\nThis document closes all 18 open questions from the design doc. It also records the full process used to decide the scoring formula weights, including 50 test scenarios and the analysis of results.\n\n---\n\n## Closed Questions\n\n### Q1 — Confirm Go and PostgreSQL\n\n**Decision:** Confirmed for Branch 2 (go-flutter). Branch 1 uses Node.js + Express + PostgreSQL. Both branches use PostgreSQL. See `techstack.md` for the full two-branch plan.\n\n---\n\n### Q2 — How do weights and ranks combine?\n\n**Decision:** See the full scoring formula section below. Weights decided are w1 = 0.50, w2 = 0.35, w3 = 0.15.\n\n---\n\n### Q3 — Which repeat patterns are in v1, and how are they stored?\n\n**Decision:**\n\nSupported patterns in v1:\n- `none` — one-time task\n- `daily` — repeats every day\n- `weekly` — repeats on the same day each week\n- `weekdays` — repeats Monday through Friday only\n\nStorage: a string enum column on the Task row (`none`, `daily`, `weekly`, `weekdays`). The original task row is the template. Block rows are generated on demand for the current week only — no pre-generating infinite future rows.\n\nAnything more complex (every 2 weeks, alternate days, custom dates) is deferred to v2.\n\n---\n\n### Q4 — Time rules: smallest unit, storing UTC vs IST, week start\n\n**Decision:**\n- **Smallest time unit:** 5 minutes. All slot boundaries snap to 5-minute marks (9:00, 9:05, 9:10, etc.).\n- **Storage:** All times stored as UTC in the database. Displayed as IST in the app. IST is UTC+5:30. No DST. The conversion is always the same fixed offset. One conversion point only — the API response layer.\n- **Week start:** Monday. The 40-block weekly limit resets every Monday at 12:00 AM IST (Sunday 6:30 PM UTC).\n\n---\n\n### Q5 — How are classes entered?\n\n**Decision:** One entry form with two options the user selects:\n- One-time (happens once on a specific date and time)\n- Weekly (repeats on the same day and time every week)\n\nNo other repeat options for fixed events in v1. This covers the vast majority of college class schedules.\n\n---\n\n### Q6 — Gap rule\n\n**Decision:**\n- 15 minutes after any block under 60 minutes.\n- 25 minutes after a 60-minute block or after the third consecutive block in a row.\n\nThis is the rule from the design doc, now confirmed.\n\n---\n\n### Q7 — Extra burnout rules: meal windows, end-of-day cutoff, rest day\n\n**Decision:** All three are enforced. All three have defaults the user can change at any time in settings.\n\n| Rule | Default |\n|---|---|\n| Lunch window (no blocks) | 1:00 PM – 2:00 PM |\n| Dinner window (no blocks) | 8:00 PM – 9:00 PM |\n| End-of-day cutoff | No blocks after 10:00 PM |\n| Rest day | Sunday |\n\nThe backend reads these values from the user's settings row and enforces them the same way it enforces fixed events. If a user changes the lunch window to 12:30 PM – 1:30 PM, the scheduler respects that from the next suggestion onward.\n\n---\n\n### Q8 — Exact scoring formula\n\nAnswered in the scoring formula section below.\n\n---\n\n### Q9 — All group rules (section 11)\n\nFully resolved. See `decisions.md`.\n\n---\n\n## Scoring Formula\n\n### Formula\n\n```\npriority_score = (0.50 × urgency) + (0.35 × goal_weight_normalised) + (0.15 × goal_rank_score)\n```\n\n**Where:**\n\n- `urgency = min(1.0, 1 / days_until_deadline)`\n  - Due today = 1.0\n  - Due in 1 day = 1.0 (capped)\n  - Due in 5 days = 0.2\n  - Due in 10 days = 0.1\n\n- `goal_weight_normalised = goal_weight / 5`\n  - User sets goal weight on a scale of 1 to 5\n  - Weight 5 = 1.0, weight 1 = 0.2\n\n- `goal_rank_score = (total_goals − rank + 1) / total_goals`\n  - Rank 1 of 3 goals = 1.0 (highest)\n  - Rank 3 of 3 goals = 0.33 (lowest)\n\nHigher score = suggested first.\n\n**Tie-breaking (in order):**\n1. Earlier deadline wins.\n2. Older task (created first) wins.\n\n---\n\n### Why these weights\n\nThe three factors in the formula are urgency, goal weight, and goal rank. The question was how much each should influence the final score.\n\nThe reasoning before testing:\n- Missing a deadline is the worst outcome for a student. Urgency should be the dominant factor.\n- Goal weight is the user's own stated priority for a subject. It should matter significantly.\n- Goal rank is a tiebreaker within goals of similar weight. It should have the least influence of the three.\n\nThis reasoning suggested urgency > goal weight > goal rank, with urgency having notably more influence than the other two.\n\n---\n\n### How the weights were tested\n\nThree candidate weight sets were defined:\n\n| Set | Urgency (w1) | Goal weight (w2) | Goal rank (w3) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| A | 0.50 | 0.35 | 0.15 |\n| B | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.20 |\n| C | 0.45 | 0.35 | 0.20 |\n\nThree additional candidates were also tested:\n\n| Set | Urgency (w1) | Goal weight (w2) | Goal rank (w3) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| D | 0.55 | 0.30 | 0.15 |\n| E | 0.45 | 0.40 | 0.15 |\n| F | 0.50 | 0.30 | 0.20 |\n\nAll six were run against 50 scenarios. Each scenario defines two tasks (A and B) and states which one should be suggested first. The formula was asked to pick a winner, and the result was compared against the expected answer.\n\n---\n\n### The 50 test scenarios\n\nScenarios are grouped by what they test. Each row: scenario number, description, which task was expected to win.\n\n**Group 1 — Urgency dominates (scenarios 1–10)**\nTwo tasks with similar goal importance but different deadlines. The task linked to the higher-weight goal should win.\n\n| # | Task A | Task B | Expected |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 11 | 7 days, weight 5, rank 2 | 7 days, weight 1, rank 2 | A |\n| 12 | 5 days, weight 4, rank 2 | 5 days, weight 2, rank 2 | A |\n| 13 | 10 days, weight 5, rank 2 | 10 days, weight 2, rank 2 | A |\n| 14 | 14 days, weight 5, rank 3 | 14 days, weight 3, rank 3 | A |\n| 15 | 3 days, weight 4, rank 2 | 3 days, weight 1, rank 2 | A |\n| 16 | 7 days, weight 3, rank 1 | 7 days, weight 1, rank 1 | A |\n| 17 | 7 days, weight 5, rank 2 | 7 days, weight 4, rank 2 | A |\n| 18 | 5 days, weight 4, rank 3 | 5 days, weight 3, rank 3 | A |\n| 19 | 10 days, weight 5, rank 3 | 10 days, weight 1, rank 1 | A |\n| 20 | 7 days, weight 4, rank 3 | 7 days, weight 2, rank 1 | A |\n\n**Group 3 — Rank breaks ties (scenarios 21–25)**\nSame deadline and same goal weight. Rank is the only differentiator.\n\n| # | Task A | Task B | Expected |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 21 | 7 days, weight 3, rank 1 | 7 days, weight 3, rank 2 | A |\n| 22 | 5 days, weight 4, rank 1 | 5 days, weight 4, rank 3 | A |\n| 23 | 10 days, weight 2, rank 2 | 10 days, weight 2, rank 3 | A |\n| 24 | 7 days, weight 5, rank 1 | 7 days, weight 5, rank 2 | A |\n| 25 | 14 days, weight 1, rank 1 | 14 days, weight 1, rank 3 | A |\n\n**Group 4 — Urgency vs goal weight tradeoff (scenarios 26–35)**\nOne task is more urgent, the other is linked to a more important goal.
